The Nagastra; Garuda Comes

Stories from the Ramayana

The Nagastra; Garuda Comes

Indrajit's unseen attack and Garuda's rescue

In everyday English — Yuddha Kanda, sargas 44–50

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home.

This book is the story of the war's darkest night. The enemy cannot even be seen — and two brothers lie bound. Where there is grief, read slowly; where Garuda comes, let light into your voice.

The yellow boxes hold the characters' own words. Change your voice a little as you speak them — Indrajit hidden, Sugriva grieving, Vibhishana calm, Garuda deep.

(Purple hints) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

The green box at the end of each part — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listeners speak.

The main story of this book is Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, sargas 44–50 — the serpent-bonds and the coming of Garuda. Rama and Lakshmana are bound — but they are not dead. Anything more you may want to know is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Rama — prince of Ayodhya, bearer of the bow. Warm dark-brown skin, a calm and kind face, fully clothed, barefoot in the forest. In this book he lies bound by the serpent-noose.

Lakshmana — Rama's younger brother, slightly lighter in complexion, bow in hand. He too is bound by the serpent-noose.

Indrajit — son of Ravana, also called Meghanada. By a boon from Brahma he can turn invisible in battle — and that is his greatest weapon.

Sugriva — king of the vanaras, friend of Rama.

Hanuman — son of the Wind, minister of Sugriva, messenger of Rama. Light golden-brown fur, long tail, gentle devoted face, saffron dhoti.

Vibhishana — Ravana's younger brother, who came to Rama's side for the sake of dharma. Calm and wise.

Jambavan — the old and wise king of the bears.

Garuda — king of birds, the mount of Vishnu, enemy of serpents. A great bird with vast golden wings — a bird-king, not a man.

Sita — held captive in the Ashoka grove. Wheat-gold skin, long black braid with white jasmine flowers, small gold jhumka earrings, a thin gold nose-ring on her left nostril, a single pale saree, no crown.

Trijata — the elderly rakshasi who looks after Sita, kind and understanding.

Ravana — king of Lanka. Tall, dark-complexioned, black moustache, tall golden crown, a single head, royal robes.

1 · The Night Battle · · THE NIGHT BATTLE

The war had begun at the gates of Lanka. All day the vanaras and the rakshasas had fought — and now night was falling. Night belongs to the rakshasas — in the dark their strength grows.

Then Ravana's son Indrajit came to the field. At first he fought openly — bow in hand, riding his chariot. Angada smashed his chariot to pieces — the charioteer fell. Indrajit was cornered.

Indrajit thought to himself — “Not openly, then — I will fight hidden. Brahma's boon is with me.”

And he vanished! No chariot could be seen, no bow, not even himself. Arrows began to rain from the sky — with no one knowing where they came from. Panic spread through the vanara army.

Rama and Lakshmana shot arrows at the sky — but how can an arrow strike a body that cannot be seen? Indrajit's voice could be heard — but he was nowhere to be found.

(Read this part slowly — as if searching for something in the dark.)

Pause and think — Indrajit was losing openly — so he hid. Is fighting while hidden still fighting — or is it a trick? And when the enemy cannot be seen at all — what does bravery even mean?

2 · The Serpent Bonds · · THE SERPENT BONDS

Then Indrajit loosed his most terrible weapon — the nagastra. His arrows turned into serpents — venomous, hissing serpents — and coiled themselves around Rama and Lakshmana.

Arrow upon arrow — no part of their bodies was left free. Both brothers fell to the earth — bound by serpents, unable even to move.

The vanara army stood stunned. Sugriva, Hanuman, Angada, Jambavan — all came running. Rama and Lakshmana were breathing — but they could not rise. They were not dead — they were bound.

Hanuman said — “They are alive! Look — they are breathing. They are bound — not dead.”

But the serpents would not leave. No one could even touch them — they hissed, ready to bite. The whole army stood helpless, watching.

Pause and think — Rama and Lakshmana are not dead — they are bound. Is being bound less sad than dying — or more? And when even the greatest warrior lies bound — where does an army find its courage?

3 · Sugriva's Grief · · SUGRIVA'S GRIEF

When Sugriva saw the two brothers lying bound — his heart broke. He said — “What is left now? Rama himself lies bound — let us return to Kishkindha.”

Despair spread among the vanaras. Some sat down, some began to weep. The war stopped — as if the whole army had stopped breathing.

Then Vibhishana stepped forward and spoke in a calm voice — “Do not fear. Rama and Lakshmana are alive — and they will rise.”

“They have honoured Brahma's weapon — that is why they have fallen. Brahma's boon cannot be false — but its time will pass. Have patience.”

Vibhishana said — “Indrajit has not killed them — he has bound them. And bonds break. We only have to guard them — until they rise.”

The vanara warriors gathered around the two brothers — like a wall. No rakshasa could come near.

Pause and think — Vibhishana is Ravana's brother — yet he stands on Rama's side. Is speaking the truth also a kind of bravery — especially when everyone is in despair? And Sugriva's grief — is that defeat — or love for his friend?

4 · Ravana's Triumph · · RAVANA'S TRIUMPH

Meanwhile Indrajit returned to Lanka — his work done. He told Ravana — “Father, Rama and Lakshmana lie on the earth. The war is over.”

Ravana swelled with joy. He ordered — deck all of Lanka with flags and garlands! Send criers through the streets — Rama and Lakshmana are dead!

Ravana said — “Now show Sita too! Take her in the Pushpaka vimana — and show her the battlefield — so she understands that no one is coming to save her now.”

Ravana was certain — the victory was his. He did not know that a bound warrior is not a dead warrior.

Pause and think — Ravana announced his victory — before the war was even over. Can hurrying to celebrate also be a kind of defeat? And is it wrong to rejoice — or only to rejoice too soon?

5 · Sita and Trijata · · SITA AND TRIJATA

The rakshasis took Sita in the Pushpaka vimana — and flew over the battlefield. Below, Sita saw — Rama and Lakshmana lying on the earth, covered with arrows and serpents.

Sita's heart sank. She began to weep — “My Rama is gone! Whom shall I live for now?”

Trijata took her hand and said — “Lady, do not weep. Your husband is alive.”

“Look — his face still shines. The face of the dead does not shine like that. And this Pushpaka vimana — it does not carry a widow. You are sitting in it — that means Rama is alive.”

Sita looked again — truly, Rama's face still held the same calm light. The vanaras stood around him — as if guarding someone, not a body.

Trijata brought Sita back to the Ashoka grove. Sita still carried grief in her heart — but beside it, now, a small hope too.

Pause and think — Trijata comforted Sita with reasons — the light on his face, the rule of the vimana, the circle of vanaras. Can reason also be a comfort in a time of grief? And Trijata — a rakshasi — why has she become Sita's greatest friend?

6 · Rama Awakens · · RAMA AWAKENS

Slowly, Rama came back to his senses. He opened his eyes — and saw Lakshmana lying bound beside him. His heart filled.

Rama said — “Lakshmana! My brother! I cannot even rise — how shall I save you?”

Just then a stir ran through the camp — someone was coming! The vanaras fled in fear — “Indrajit has come again! He has come again!”

But it was not Indrajit — it was Vibhishana. He was coming to meet Rama — but the vanaras saw him and thought Indrajit had returned.

Jambavan called out loudly — “Stop! Do not fear! This is Vibhishana — Rama's friend! Not Indrajit!”

The vanaras stopped. Vibhishana came to Rama — and said to Sugriva — “Have patience. Rama will rise. This bond will not last forever.”

Pause and think — The vanaras feared Vibhishana — because he looked like Indrajit? Can fear sometimes make us afraid of our own friend? And Jambavan's voice — the voice of an elder — how does it calm everyone?

7 · Garuda Comes · · GARUDA COMES

Then a brightness flashed in the sky — like a tongue of flame! A great bird was descending — wings so vast they covered the sky. It was Garuda — king of birds.

At the very sight of Garuda, the serpents began to flee! The serpents coiled around Rama and Lakshmana loosened their hold and fled. Garuda is the enemy of serpents — his coming itself is fear to them.

Garuda touched both brothers with his wings — and their wounds began to heal. The arrows that had pierced them came out. Their bodies became whole and fair again.

Garuda said — “Rama, I am your friend — like your own breath. You were bound by Indrajit's trickery — now you are free.”

(Let light into your voice here — as if morning is coming.)

Pause and think — Garuda fought no battle — he only came — and the serpents fled. Is someone's coming alone sometimes enough? And the bird-king, enemy of serpents — does nature itself hold a cure for every poison?

8 · Freedom and the Roar · · FREEDOM AND THE ROAR

Garuda embraced Rama — and flew away into the sky. Rama and Lakshmana rose to their feet — as if waking from sleep. No wound remained on their bodies.

Rama said — “Garuda, without you we would never have escaped this bond. We will never forget this kindness.”

A wave of joy ran through the vanara army. All began to roar — like lions! Tails waved, drums beat.

And then the whole army marched toward the gates of Lanka — to fight again. Ravana's announcement had proved false — Rama was alive, and the war was not yet over.

But Ravana — in his palace — still believed that Rama was dead.

Pause and think — Garuda has gone — but he left something behind — freedom. Is freedom also a kind of strength? And when an army roars again — is that roar only joy — or also the preparation for war?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main source

The main story of this book is Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, sargas 44–50 — the serpent-bonds and the coming of Garuda.

The night battle — sarga 44

Indrajit fighting openly; Angada smashing his chariot; then, by Brahma's boon, turning invisible and raining arrows — this is in sarga 44.

The serpent-bonds — sarga 45

The arrows of the nagastra turning into serpents and coiling around Rama and Lakshmana; both brothers falling to the earth — this is in sarga 45.

Sugriva's grief — sarga 46

Sugriva losing heart and speaking of returning to Kishkindha; Vibhishana comforting him, saying the brothers live and have only honoured Brahma's weapon — this is in sarga 46.

Showing Sita the field — sarga 47

Indrajit returning to Lanka with news of victory; Ravana decking Lanka and proclaiming the victory; Sita taken in the Pushpaka vimana to see the bound brothers — this is in sarga 47.

Trijata's comfort — sarga 48

Sita's lament; Trijata comforting her, saying Rama lives — the light on his face and the rule of the Pushpaka vimana are the proof; then bringing Sita back to the Ashoka grove — this is in sarga 48.

Rama awakens — sarga 49

Rama coming back to his senses and weeping for Lakshmana — this is in sarga 49.

Vibhishana's arrival, and Garuda — sarga 50

The vanaras mistaking the arriving Vibhishana for Indrajit and fleeing in fear; Jambavan calming them; Garuda coming, the serpents fleeing, the brothers healed; Garuda speaking with Rama and flying away; the vanaras roaring and marching to Lanka's gates — this is in sarga 50.

Bound — not dead

In this book Rama and Lakshmana are bound — not dead. The pictures too show them lying down — not lifeless. No death, body, or blood is shown in any picture.

What happens next

Ravana is about to learn that Rama is alive — and he will send his generals, one by one. The stories of Dhumraksha, Vajradamshtra, Akampana and Prahasta are in the next book of this series.
